stances.claim: Responding to online comments -- even outrageous, malicious, or hideous ones -- is generally unnecessary because Inquirer's 'Balanced News, Fearless Views' policy lets comments balance and correct one another, and 'stoic silence washes more than a torrent of invectives'; only gutter language with cybercrime liability warrants legal action.
stances.rhetorical_move: silence-as-strategy (positioning non-response as discipline rather than disengagement)

stances.claim: CJ refuses long-distance legal advice because (Holmes) 'general propositions do not decide concrete cases' -- every case requires specific facts and applicable laws; readers should consult licensed counsel, PAO, or IBP.
stances.rhetorical_move: Holmes-citation principle (anchoring practical refusal in jurisprudential authority)

stances.claim: CJ refused to rejoin law practice after retirement, even as 'of counsel,' because his appearance before judges who had served under him could create perception of bias -- especially if he won -- making post-judicial private practice a perception-tax that the office cannot absorb.
stances.rhetorical_move: perception-as-ethics (extending recusal logic past the bench into post-retirement life)

stances.claim: Hostile reader questions deserve good-faith, evidenced answers -- CJ's chief-justice record is documented in his annual books, the Court library, and the unanimous Plaque of Acclamation signed by all 14 associate justices in 2006, and his personal docket fell from 1,100 + 45/month to 200 current cases at retirement.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidence-of-record rebuttal (responding to ad hominem with documentary proof)
stances.confidence: asserted with citations to his own books and the Plaque

stances.claim: Fair disagreement -- even from justices, generals, or readers -- deserves printing rather than suppression, and the best response to a colleague's challenge is to honor their accomplishments rather than to retaliate.
stances.rhetorical_move: magnanimity-in-disagreement (publishing opposing views and lauding their authors)

notable_anecdotes: CJ's correction to his own quoted reply (in brackets in the column): the initial docket was 1,100 not 1,200, and the monthly accretion was 45 not 30 -- the rare moment when CJ visibly amends a previously-given factual claim in real time within the same column.
Justice Antonio T. Carpio's tribute on CJ's retirement: 'Chief Justice Panganiban is the Court's most prolific writer, bar none' -- invoked here as documentary evidence rather than mere flattery.
The 'Plaque of Acclamation signed unanimously by all the 14 associate justices' as the most institutionally weighty endorsement of CJ's chief-justice record, hosted on cjpanganiban.com.
Gen. Antonio Sotelo's quip 'If 10 lawyers read your article, you will receive 11 opinions' -- affectionately included as evidence that legal pluralism is unavoidable.

Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez's email -- 'Chief, thank you but I wonder why you keep citing me and my decision in David v. Arroyo' -- answered by CJ with one of his most memorable single-line tributes: 'your career and your decision exemplify how to rise from human mortality to judicial immortality.'

The hostile reader closing with 'be humble enough' invoking God -- and CJ replying without meanness, demonstrating his stated policy that 'I invariably assume good faith, and answer without meanness.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why he generally declines to respond to online comments -- Inquirer's 'Balanced News, Fearless Views' policy lets comments balance one another, and 'stoic silence washes more than a torrent of invectives,' though he will sue violators of the cybercrime law. Citing Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. ('General propositions do not decide concrete cases'), he refuses to dispense long-distance legal advice and instead refers readers to licensed counsel, the Public Attorney's Office, or the IBP. He reiterates that he dissolved his law office on joining the Court and has not rejoined any firm post-retirement -- even as 'of counsel' -- because his appearance before judges who had served under him would create perception of bias. He then reproduces verbatim a hostile reader's five-question email and prints his straight answers to questions 2 and 4 about his own chief-justice record: he retired with no backlog in his personal docket, reducing his caseload from 1,100 initial cases (plus 45 raffled monthly) to 200 current cases, and instituted 'Operation Zero Backlog' across the entire Court -- facts documented in his annual books (one per year of incumbency), in the Supreme Court library, and on cjpanganiban.com, where the Plaque of Acclamation signed unanimously by all 14 associate justices is hosted. He closes by appreciating dissenting reactions to his recent columns -- Justice Adolf S. Azcuna's text disagreement on the MDT and Hickenlooper Amendment, Gen. Antonio Sotelo's '10 lawyers, 11 opinions' quip, and Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez's wonder at his frequent citation of her David v. Arroyo ponencia -- with his memorable rejoinder: 'I will not cease doing so because your career and your decision exemplify how to rise from human mortality to judicial immortality.'
